title: Why the Apple Newton Failed and What It's Worth Now
body:
The Apple Newton was Apple's handheld computer line, launched on August 2, 1993 at $699 and canceled by Steve Jobs on February 27, 1998. It failed because the handwriting recognition did not work at launch, the price never came down, and a $299 PalmPilot did the same job reliably from the first day. The Newton is gone for good: there has been no Newton device and no Newton OS release since 1998, Apple Inc. still owns the name, and a complete MessagePad 2100 sold for $541 at auction in 2023.

Quick facts
Launched
August 2, 1993, Apple Computer, $699
Status today
Discontinued February 27, 1998; no Newton device or Newton OS release since
Owner today
Apple Inc., which still owns the Newton name
Units sold
50,000 MessagePads in the US and Europe by the end of September 1993
Price today
$541 for a complete MessagePad 2100 at RR Auction in 2023; $1,880 for an unused one

Has Apple been profitable ever since the Newton died?

What people type into Google is whether Apple has been in the black every year since it killed the Apple Newton. Almost. There is one break in the run.

Apple lost $1.045 billion in fiscal 1997. In fiscal 1998, the year the Newton was canceled, it earned $309 million. Fiscal 1999 brought $601 million and fiscal 2000 brought $786 million.

Then fiscal 2001 broke the streak with a net loss of $25 million, on net sales of $5.363 billion against $7.983 billion the year before. Both figures sit in the five-year table of Apple's Form 10-K405 for the year ended September 29, 2001. That year is the part left out whenever someone says Apple has been profitable since 1998.

The turnaround was real all the same. Apple spent the middle of the 1990s burning through cash it did not have, and fiscal 1998 was also the year of the first iMac. The Newton was cut in the same twelve months the company returned to profit.

What went wrong with Newton handwriting recognition?

John Sculley, then Apple's chief executive, put the phrase personal digital assistant into circulation at the Consumer Electronics Show in Las Vegas in January 1992, and showed a Newton prototype at the summer show in Chicago on May 29, 1992.

The first MessagePad reached buyers on August 2, 1993 at $699. The promise was that it would read ordinary handwriting with no training and no special alphabet, using a recognition engine Apple licensed from ParaGraph International.

It did not. The recognizer guessed at words, and it guessed wrong often enough that the failure became the product's public identity inside a month. A Doonesbury strip in August 1993 showed the machine turning a line of handwriting into "Egg Freckles," and the phrase followed the Newton for the rest of its life.

Sales never recovered from the reviews. Apple said 50,000 MessagePads had sold in the United States and Europe by the end of September 1993, and later accounts put the same milestone in late November. Either way it was not enough to carry a new platform, and the price never came down to meet the market: the last model, the MessagePad 2100, arrived in November 1997 at about $1,000.

Is the Apple Newton still around in 2026?

No. Steve Jobs canceled the Newton hardware and the Newton OS platform on February 27, 1998, months after returning to run the company. The announcement took the MessagePad 2100 and the eMate 300, the keyboard model Apple had introduced for schools on March 7, 1997 at $799, off the price list together.

The reason was stated plainly at the time. "This decision is consistent with our strategy to focus all of our software development resources on extending the Macintosh operating system," Jobs said in Apple's announcement of February 27, 1998. He added that "to realize our ambitious plans we must focus all of our efforts in one direction."

There has been no Newton device and no Newton OS release since. Apple Inc. still exists and still owns the name, but it did not sell another pocket computer until the iPhone in 2007, and nothing in the current lineup carries the Newton brand.

Where to find one today. Complete MessagePads are what hold value. RR Auction sold a fully accessorized MessagePad 2100, with its box, power adapter, stylus, battery packs, cables and keyboard, for $541 at its August 2023 Apple sale against a $200 estimate, and its lot record for an unused 2100 still sealed in its original plastic shows $1,880 against a $600 estimate. Tested units with no box and no accessories go for a fraction of that, and vintage sellers list them on Etsy. A corroded battery pack is the most common thing wrong with a listing.

Can you still use a Newton MessagePad in 2026?

Yes, with a patch. Newton OS keeps time in a 30-bit count of seconds, and that counter ran out at 6:48 pm on January 5, 2010, which left unpatched machines mangling dates and alarms.

Apple had been out of the business for twelve years by then, so owners fixed it themselves. Eckhart Koppen and Paul Guyot wrote system patches for the MessagePad 2000 and 2100, and Avi Drissman's Fix2010 package covered older Newton OS 2.0 machines such as the MessagePad 120 and 130. Guyot's earlier system update was the first one for the platform that Apple had neither written nor shipped.

The fixes are not perfect. Owners reported that one version sent the clock back to 2008 after a reset, which a later patch corrected.

The other route is emulation. Einstein, an open-source Newton OS emulator, builds for macOS, Linux, iOS and Android, and needs a MessagePad 2100 ROM image that it does not ship.

How a $299 PalmPilot took the market Apple defined

Palm Computing's answer was to stop trying to read natural handwriting at all. Its Graffiti system made the user learn a simplified stroke alphabet, one motion per letter, inside a fixed box on the screen. It asked less of the machine and more of the owner, and it was reliable from the first day.

Price finished the argument. The Pilot 1000 shipped in March 1996 at $299, with the 512 KB Pilot 5000 at $369. Apple was asking $699 for the original MessagePad and about $1,000 for the 2100.

Apple did fix the product, too late to matter. Newton OS 2.0 dropped the licensed engine for a recognizer Apple wrote itself, and the MessagePad 2000 of March 1997 ran a StrongARM processor at about 162 MHz, roughly ten times the speed of the first model.

So the category Apple had named and spent four years defining went to a cheaper device that did fewer things and did not embarrass its owner in a meeting. Palm took the handheld market the Newton had been built for, and Apple was out of it by February 1998.

The ARM stake that outlasted the MessagePad

The Newton needed a processor that could run all day on batteries, and nothing on the market managed it, so Apple went in with Acorn Computers and VLSI Technology in November 1990 on the chip venture then called Advanced RISC Machines. The MessagePad was the first Apple product to ship with the result: a 20 MHz ARM 610 behind a 336 by 240 monochrome screen, with 640 KB of RAM.

The stake turned out to be worth more than the product it was bought for. Apple sold ARM Holdings shares in every quarter of fiscal 2000. Its results of January 19, 2000 included "an after-tax gain of $101 million resulting from the sale of approximately five million shares of ARM Holdings plc," and the quarter after that added $73 million more.

That single quarter's gain was a third of the company's entire fiscal 1998 profit of $309 million, out of shares bought to get a chip for a 1993 handheld. The instruction set Apple went shopping for because a pocket computer had to last a day on batteries now runs every iPhone and every Mac built on Apple silicon.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is an Apple Newton worth today?

Complete examples do best. RR Auction sold an Apple Newton MessagePad 2100 with its box, power adapter, stylus, battery packs, cables and keyboard for $541 at its August 2023 Apple sale, against a pre-sale estimate of $200, and its lot record for an unused 2100 sealed in its original plastic shows $1,880. A loose MessagePad with no box and no accessories sells for a fraction of either.

Why did Steve Jobs kill the Apple Newton?

Steve Jobs canceled the Apple Newton platform on February 27, 1998, months after returning to a company that had lost $1.045 billion in fiscal 1997. He said the decision was "consistent with our strategy to focus all of our software development resources on extending the Macintosh operating system," and a slow-selling MessagePad 2100 at about $1,000 was an easy cut.

Has Apple been profitable every year since 1998?

Not quite. Apple reported net income of $309 million in fiscal 1998, $601 million in fiscal 1999 and $786 million in fiscal 2000, then a net loss of $25 million in fiscal 2001. The Apple Newton was canceled in February 1998, in the first of those profitable years.
